text: A well-written ADR and a clean diagram are both snapshots -- accurate the day they're written, and only as accurate as the system stays unchanged afterward. This lesson is about the part that actually keeps them honest over time: where they live, what forces a review, and how an ADR is allowed to go out of date without quietly lying.

The fix that scales is physical, not procedural: put docs/adr right in the same repository as the Terraform and Bicep code from Chapter 2, next to landing-zone, network, and modules. That gets you three things a separate wiki never does -- ADRs versioned in the same git history as the code, a pull request that touches the infrastructure that can be required to touch or reference the matching ADR, and decisions that surface automatically in the same searchable codebase instead of a wiki nobody thought to check.

A quarterly calendar reminder to review the docs is the first thing a busy team skips -- and a busy team is exactly the one whose documentation needs the most attention. The durable version ties the review to the change itself: a pull request checklist item for anything touching network or landing-zone, a required reviewer on docs/adr for RTO, RPO, or boundary changes, and a link from the PR back to the ADR it implements, so a reviewer can confirm the change actually matches what was decided.

An outdated ADR isn't a bug to fix by deleting the file. It moves through a status instead: Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated when it's no longer followed, or Superseded by a specific later ADR, with both records kept and cross-linked. Deleting the old one would recreate the exact oral-history problem this chapter opened with.

That closes Chapter 6: a written record for every real decision, a consistent way to draw it, and a way to keep both from rotting. Chapter 7 puts this to work for real -- presenting and defending an architecture in front of a review board that will ask exactly the questions this chapter prepared you to answer.
